Fix scores, eligibility, and deterministic score-and-item-ID ordering. Of N eligible negatives, exactly K precede the positive. Uniformly sampling m distinct negatives gives X ~ Hypergeometric(N,K,m): P(X=x)=C(K,x)C(N−K,m−x)/C(N,m). The positive’s sampled rank is X+1, so its realized HR@10 is 1{X≤9}, and its expected sampled HR@10 is P(X≤9), obtained by summing that probability over x=0,…,min(9,K,m), with infeasible binomial coefficients treated as zero. Average these probabilities across users for the exact expected sampled metric; repeated candidate resampling is unnecessary when N and K are known.

Krichene and Rendle’s [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) (KDD 2020) shows that sampled metrics can reverse aggregate model comparisons even in expectation. The hypergeometric calculation specializes that sampling framework to sampling without replacement: it replaces the full-catalog hit indicator 1{K≤9} with a smooth sampling probability. Averaging more candidate draws estimates this different quantity more precisely; it does not recover full-catalog HR@10.

Disagreement therefore establishes sensitivity to candidate-set size or composition, not an implementation failure or superior full-catalog performance. Under identical eligibility, scores, and ordering, every full-catalog hit must remain a sampled hit, while a full-catalog miss can become a sampled hit. Violations of that implication, or statistically implausible deviations from the exact sampling baseline, justify investigating scoring, filtering, ties, or sampling. The formula assumes uniform sampling without replacement; nonuniform or duplicate-containing candidate generation requires a different baseline.
